title: US federal monthly deficit, July 2026
question: What will the U.S. Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service first report as the federal government's current-month deficit or surplus for July 2026 in Monthly Treasury Statement Table 1, in nominal USD billions, with deficits positive and surpluses negative?
resolutionRule: Resolve to the July 2026 current-month Total Surplus (+) or Deficit (-) in the first official U.S. Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service Monthly Treasury Statement Table 1 print, converted from millions to billions of nominal dollars and sign-flipped so deficits are positive and surpluses are negative. Use the first published MTS table; later revisions or FiscalData refreshes do not change the resolved value unless Treasury replaces the first table on the same publication date.

drivers: July usually has no major individual or corporate tax due date
benefit and Medicare outlays continue to trend upward in nominal dollars
August 1, 2026 falls on a Saturday, likely pulling some August payments into July
elevated customs receipts reduce the deficit relative to gross-outlay pressure
refund and tariff-refund timing can move the monthly balance materially

reasoning.text: Forecast for July 2026 Monthly Treasury Statement deficit

The target is the first official Treasury MTS Table 1 current-month deficit/surplus for July 2026, in USD billions, with deficits reported as positive values. I treat FiscalData/MTS as the resolver and do not use later revisions.

reasoning.text: Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the clean outside view is recent official July MTS first prints. July 2022-2024 deficits were 211.052, 220.782, and 243.741 billion, averaging about 225.2 billion, with a rising but still fairly tight pre-2026 range.

Level, momentum, and mechanism: nominal outlays should be above the 2022-2024 level because Social Security, Medicare, health, and net interest are higher. July 2026 also has an important calendar feature: August 1 falls on a Saturday, so payments normally due August 1 can be made on July 31, lifting July outlays relative to ordinary July months. Elevated tariff/customs receipts partly offset that, but May 2026 context suggests refunds and tariff refunds can also absorb some gross receipts.

Prior/update/interval: prior model is recent-July first-print persistence using the 2022-2024 official MTS sample, centered at 225.2 billion. I add about 45 billion for nominal benefit, health, and interest growth versus the 2024 July outlay base, add about 55 billion for August-1 payment acceleration into July 2026, and subtract about 15 billion for elevated customs receipts net of refund risk, giving about 310 billion. The 80% interval starts from realized July dispersion of roughly 211 to 244 billion, then widens strongly for the calendar-payment shock, tariff/refund uncertainty, and missing June 2026 official print before this run.

Counter-consideration: the downside case is that payment acceleration is smaller than expected and tariff/customs collections remain high, pushing the print toward the 2024-like low 200s. The upside case is that August-payment acceleration is large, refunds are heavy, or interest/health outlays jump, pushing the deficit above 400 billion. Outside the interval would likely require either an unusually clean low-refund/high-receipt month below 170 billion or a very large payment/refund timing shock above 470 billion.

Calculation: recent-July prior average = (211.052 + 220.782 + 243.741) / 3 = 225.2 billion. Updates: +45 for nominal outlay growth, +55 for August 1 payment acceleration into July, -15 for customs/tariff receipt offset, equals 310.2, rounded to 310. Interval: 310 - 140 = 170 and 310 + 160 = 470, asymmetric to allow a fatter high-deficit payment-timing tail.
